extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated readers interested in species distribution and evolution
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria and evidential tests for explaining the geographic distribution of species (single vs multiple origins, modes of dispersal, and the effects of past climates and geology). Focuses on when to infer migration, what agents could effect dispersal, and how past geological/climatic events shape present distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-origin rule for species
rubrics_metrics.description: Each species was most probably produced in one area alone and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view is preferred for its simplicity and because rejecting it requires invoking miracles; continuity of range in most species supports the single-birthplace inference. Exceptions exist but are not, by themselves, sufficient to overturn the general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of range as evidence of migration
rubrics_metrics.description: If the area inhabited by a species is continuous, this supports the idea it migrated from a single birthplace rather than being independently created in multiple places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When species are found in distant points with intervening inhospitable tracts, those cases are treated as exceptional and require special explanation (past continuity, unusual dispersal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers indicate local origination
rubrics_metrics.description: The striking influence of physical barriers on distribution indicates that the majority of species have been produced on one side of a barrier and have not crossed to the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High incidence of families/genera confined to a single region, and the locality of the most 'natural' (closely related) genera, support inferring origin on one side of barriers rather than repeated independent creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic closeness implies common source or stocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Regions whose inhabitants are closely related (many species belonging to the same genera) probably received immigrants from the related region at some former period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the principle of modification, descendants of colonists will be plainly related to the inhabitants of the source region even after modification; such relationships strengthen migration/stocking hypotheses over independent creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical individuals cannot arise independently by natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is incredible that individuals identically the same should have been produced through natural selection from parents specifically distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore identical individuals found in distant regions imply common ancestry and migration from a single original spot, not independent origin in multiple spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential dispersal capacities across taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of organisms have very different capacities for crossing barriers (e.g., terrestrial mammals rarely cross seas; many plants have varied means of dispersal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of the same mammal on distant continents should be attributed to limited migration ability rather than multiple origins; plants' greater dispersal explains more widespread identical occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use past geological and climatic change to explain current distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes of climate and changes of land level (e.g., former land bridges, sunken islands) must be considered as powerful influences on migration and distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of whether migration could have occurred should incorporate evidence for former connections or climate regimes; but extraordinary claims of continent-scale recent unions require strong geological support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about vast recent continental unions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that almost every island was recently connected with continents (Forbes' extreme view) should be critically evaluated against evidence such as marine faunal differences, tertiary relationships, sea-depth correlations, and islands' volcanic composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept massive geographic revolutions within the recent period unless supported by multiple lines of geological and biogeographical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed flotation and salt-water resistance experiments as quantitative plausibility tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental results (e.g., 64/87 seeds germinated after 28 days' immersion; 18/94 dried fruits floated >28 days and germinated) provide quantitative inputs to estimate how many seeds of a flora might survive sea transport over given durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin infers from his and others' experiments that roughly 10–14% of seeds of a flora might be capable of surviving ~28–42 days and thus be floated across ~900 miles; such empirical estimates should be used to judge plausibility of seed-mediated dispersal across oceans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drift timber and enclosed soil as rafting mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Drift timber that carries embedded stones and pockets of earth can protect and carry seeds and even seedlings over long distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of plants germinating from soil completely enclosed in roots of driftwood indicate rafting can transport viable propagules intact; include this mechanism when explaining island colonization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birds as seed vectors (external and internal transport)
rubrics_metrics.description: Living birds can transport seeds externally (mud on feet), internally in crops and gizzards, and via pellets; seeds in bird crops may remain viable for many hours and sometimes days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider flying distance (birds can be blown long distances), retention times (12–30+ hours in crops/stomachs), and instances of seeds germinating after passage when assessing bird-mediated dispersal; even rare events accumulate over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil adhering to bird feet and mass migrations as rare but real dispersal events
rubrics_metrics.description: Soil and seeds adhering to the feet of migrating birds (e.g., millions of quails crossing the Mediterranean) can occasionally transport seeds great distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though individual probability is small, the large numbers and repeated migrations make such events plausible contributors to long-distance colonization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeds transported via fish-bird-fish trophic chain
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeds eaten by freshwater fish can survive inside fish, and when those fish are eaten by birds, seeds may be passed on and remain viable (pellets or excrement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include complex biological transfer chains as possible dispersal pathways in particular contexts (freshwater to aerial carriers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Icebergs and glacial transport as agents for polar and glacial-era dispersal
rubrics_metrics.description: Icebergs can be loaded with earth, stones, brushwood, bones, and nests, and so may transport seeds between arctic/antarctic regions and during glacial periods between temperate areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of erratic boulders and exotic rocks on oceanic islands (e.g., Azores) supports iceberg-mediated transport; consider this especially for polar/alpine floras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative low-probability events over geological time
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional or 'accidental' means of transport (currents, gales, rafting, birds, ice) acting year after year for centuries or thousands of years can produce substantial dispersal despite low per-event probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss rare mechanisms because each event is unlikely; integrate frequency over long timescales when estimating colonization probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limits of occasional dispersal mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The described mechanisms can account for crossing hundreds of miles, island-to-mainland transfers, and mixing over geological times, but are insufficient to explain wholesale mingling of floras across widely separated continents in short times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these mechanisms to explain island colonization and moderate long-distance dispersal, but rely on deeper-time connections or different explanations for near-complete continental mixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glacial-cycle model for identical alpine/arctic species on distant summits
rubrics_metrics.description: During glacial maxima, arctic species migrated south and occupied lowlands; when warmth returned, they retreated to mountain summits, leaving identical species isolated on distant mountains — explaining identical alpine/arctic species at remote sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the succession of glacial advance and retreat to explain both identity (mass migration together) and subsequent isolation; this model predicts affinities of alpine flora to the arctic flora of the direction from which migrants came.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential modification based on isolation history
rubrics_metrics.description: Arctic forms that migrated en masse and remained together are less likely to have been modified; alpine productions left isolated on different mountains are more likely to have been modified, producing varieties, doubtful forms, or representative species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater divergence among isolated alpine populations than among populations that remained united during range shifts; use degree of modification to infer isolation duration and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of earlier (Pliocene) warm periods to explain Northern Hemisphere affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: A warmer Pliocene with more continuous circumpolar land allowed intermixture of northern faunas and floras of Old and New Worlds, explaining observed affinities and representative forms now separated by ocean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke earlier warm-stage land continuity when explaining broader Old/New World relationships that cannot be accounted for by recent occasional dispersal alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative/related (not identical) species arise from ancient shared ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Where closely allied but distinct species occur on separated continents or shores, this can be explained by common ancestral populations that migrated and then diverged in different regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret many trans-continental taxonomic resemblances as the result of ancient connectivity followed by subsequent migration and modification, rather than independent creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Island composition and biota as evidence against sunken-continent hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Oceanic islands' predominantly volcanic composition and their faunal/floral characteristics argue against their being remnants of sunken continents and thus against excessively extensive recent land continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When weighing claims that islands were formerly continuous with continents, consider island geology and biotic evidence (volcanic origin, fauna differences) which typically disfavor sunken-continent explanations.
